State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP 9736-12
AGENCY DKT. NO.
JOHN WEINLEIN,
Petitioner,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMEN’S
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
__________________________
John D. Feeley, Esq., petitioner
Jeremy M. Vaida, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (John J. Hoffman, Acting Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: June 27, 2014 Decided: November 10, 2014
BEFORE ROBERT BINGHAM II, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Petitioner John Weinlein appeals a denial of accidental disability retirement benefits on grounds that the traumatic event was not
undesigned and unexpected. On July 27, 2011, petitioner filed an application for disability retirement due to work-related injuries
sustained on December 20, 2009. On May 14, 2012, respondent, the Board of Trustees of the Police and Firemen’s Retirement
System (the Board or PFRS), denied petitioner’s application for accidental disability benefits and approved ordinary disability
instead. Petitioner filed a timely appeal and the matter was transmitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL), where it was

filed on July 18, 2012. N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to 15; N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -13. The hearing was held on May 19, 2014, and the
record remained open for post-hearing submissions. The record closed on June 27, 2014, upon receipt of the final post-hearing
submission, and extensions were granted until November 10, 2014, for issuance of this decision.
FACTUAL DISCUSSION
Weinlein was enrolled in the PFRS on or about September 21, 1979.( J-2.) In December 2009 he was chief of police of
the Township of Berkeley. The pertinent civil-service job specification for police chief (J-5) lists his duties including, for example,
provision of assistance for traffic emergencies.
On December 20, 2009, Weinlein injured his left arm and shoulder when, in the performance of his duties, he pushed the
rear of a snow-stuck car that lurched forward and caused him to fall. (P-1.) Consequently, on July 27, 2011, he filed an
application for accidental disability retirement based upon the injury. (J-3.) On May 14, 2012, the PFRS denied petitioner’s
application for accidental disability benefits, but approved ordinary disability. Specifically, the Board determined that the
petitioner was totally and permanently disabled from the performance of his regular and assigned duties, and that he was
physically or mentally incapacitated from the performance of his usual or other duties that his employer was willing to offer. The
Board also specifically determined that the causal event: (1) was identifiable as to time and place; (2) was caused by a
circumstance external to petitioner and was not the result of pre-existing disease; (3) occurred during and as a result of his
regular and assigned duties; and (4) did not involve an injury resulting from willful negligence. The Board based its denial upon a
determination that the incident that caused petitioner’s disability claim was not undesigned and unexpected. (J-6.) I FIND as
FACT the above undisputed evidence.
John Weinlein testified that on December 22, 2009, as police chief of Berkeley Township, he was involved with a work-
related accident while assisting with the removal of a vehicle from a snow embankment. He had responded to a call to assist a
woman who had a scheduled medical procedure, but whose car was stuck in the snow. As he assisted by pushing the rear of the
vehicle, rocking it back and forth, the car suddenly lurched forward, causing him to fall to the ground. (P-1; P-2.) He assumes the
driver had hit the gas pedal because the wheels were spinning when the car lurched forward. He landed on his left arm,
impacting his left shoulder. Though he had performed such service many times before, never had he encountered such an
occurrence. But for the accident, he would have continued to work until retirement at age sixty-five.
On cross-examination, Weinlein testified that, over the course of thirty-two years, he had assisted people with getting out
of the snow on ten to fifteen occasions. Though he was familiar with pushing cars, and had pushed perhaps one hundred cars,
including in conditions of mud and snow, nothing like this had ever happened before. He had experienced cars unable to escape
such an area, with acceleration of the gas, but never an incident when a car lurched forward like that.
In his experience, car wheels can spin upon acceleration when stuck in snow, but usually when the wheels are spinning,
the car does not escape that situation, though it may ultimately do so. In his experience, a car is usually freed by a front tow,
placement of something under it, or other ways that are not abrupt as occurred here. On this occasion, he did not place blocks
under the wheels and, if anything, would have used something that would create friction, like a rug.
Based upon the testimony and exhibits, as well as the opportunity to observe the appearance and demeanor of the witness, I
further FIND the following as FACT:
In the performance of his duties as police chief, petitioner had knowledge and experience regarding the removal of motor
vehicles from entrapment in snow. On numerous occasions he had assisted with such maneuvers, including the pushing of
vehicles. In his experience, even when car wheels spin in snow, a car does not suddenly lurch forward. However, on December
20, 2009, the vehicle that he attempted to extricate from the snow, by pushing it from the rear, lurched forward suddenly, with the
wheels spinning. The driver had accelerated, causing an unexpected and abrupt movement of the car that caused petitioner to

fall and injure his shoulder. Petitioner did not have a pre-existing condition.
Petitioner contends that the incident was undesigned and unexpected; the mere possibility that he could have anticipated
the car lurching forward does not preclude the incident from being an undesigned and unexpected traumatic event. Respondent
contends that the incident was foreseeable and simply the result of strenuous work effort, which is insufficient to render it
undesigned and unexpected.
LEGAL ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSION
In order to qualify for accidental disability retirement benefits, a member of the PFRS must be permanently and totally disabled
as a direct result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his or her regular or assigned duties.
N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. In Richardson v. Board of Trustees, PFRS, 192 N.J. 189 (2007), the New Jersey Supreme Court set the
current standard for accidental disability benefits, whereby a member who has demonstrated permanent and total disability must
1
also prove, in pertinent part, that the disability is
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and unexpected, and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease
that is aggravated or accelerated by the work).
[192 N.J. at 212–13.]
The Court stated that “a member who is injured as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap has satisfied the
traumatic event standard.” Id. at 213. It gave the examples of a police officer who suffers a total and permanent disability from a
fall while chasing a suspect, or a gym teacher who “trips over a riser and is injured.” Ibid. The Court emphasized that a traumatic
event can occur during ordinary work effort in the course of regular or assigned duties. By way of example, “[a] policeman can be
shot while pursuing a suspect; a librarian can be hit by a falling bookshelf while re-shelving books; a social worker can catch her
hand in the car door while transporting a child to court,” and each scenario is “undesigned and unexpected.” Id. at 214.
The polestar of the inquiry is whether, during the regular performance of his job, an unexpected
happening, not the result of pre-existing disease alone or in combination with the work, has occurred
and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability of the member.
[Ibid.]
In Brooks v. Board of Trustees, Public Employees’ Retirement System, 425 N.J. Super. 277 (App. Div. 2012), cited by
petitioner, the court further explained the Richardson tests, particularly the requirement that a work-connected event must be
“undesigned and unexpected” to constitute a “traumatic event.” In Brooks, a school custodian was injured when he attempted to

support one end of a heavy weight bench after students, who had been carrying the other end, suddenly dropped it, causing
disabling injuries to the custodian’s shoulder. The administrative law judge (ALJ) and the Board found that the event was not
“undesigned and unexpected,” reasoning that the custodian should have anticipated that such an event could have occurred and
that he was negligent by not taking action to avoid this foreseeable event. The court held that an accident can be “undesigned
and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in retrospect that the employee could have
anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to avoid it. Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284. And an applicant’s
“simple negligence” that is a contributing cause to the incident, as opposed to “willful negligence,” is not a disqualifying factor.
The applicant need only show a “total and permanently disabling injury ‘as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated
mishap.’” Id. at 284–85 (quoting Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213).
In the unreported decision of Onesti v. Board of Trustees, PFRS, No. A-2791-11 (App. Div. March 27, 2013),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, a police officer injured his hand while using a staple gun to reattach a paper target
during a firearms-qualification test. The Board denied accidental disability benefits on the grounds that the disability was not the
result of a traumatic event, as the incident was not “undesigned and unexpected,” and the disability was the “result of his willful
negligence.” The Board subsequently rejected the ALJ’s determination that the incident was an accident that produced “a totally
unexpected consequence,” and concluded instead that petitioner’s own negligence in failing to examine the staple gun made his
injury “reasonably foreseeable and thus not undesigned and unexpected.” The court reversed and remanded the matter to the
Board for reconsideration in light of the Brooks decision, which had been reported while the case was on appeal.
Here, the Board argues that the injury did not result from an undesigned and unexpected event because it was a
foreseeable consequence of a routine task, and was at best the result of strenuous work effort. The Board cites Cattani v. Board
of Trustees, PFRS, 69 N.J. 578 (1976), as support for the proposition that strenuous work effort does not constitute an
undesigned and unexpected traumatic event. However, in Cattani, accidental disability benefits were denied to a firefighter who
had heart disease and was disabled when he performed unusually strenuous firefighting activity, because aggravation of a pre-
existing condition was not a traumatic event regardless of whether the work effort was usual or unusual.
This matter does not involve any contributing prior medical condition or extraordinary work effort, as in Cattani. Here,
there indeed was an external traumatic event without any aggravation of pre-existing illness. Rather, petitioner responded in the
course of his duties to assist someone who had a medical appointment in freeing her car from the snow. He pushed the car from
the rear, and it lurched forward suddenly, with the wheels spinning. The driver had accelerated, causing an unexpected and
abrupt movement of the car that caused petitioner to fall and injure his shoulder. Indeed, the event was an “‘identifiable,
unanticipated mishap.’” Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284–85 (quoting Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213).
Simply put, “during the regular performance of his job, an unexpected happening, not the result of pre-existing disease
alone or in combination with the work, has occurred and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability of the member.”
Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 214. As stated in Brooks:
The ALJ, whose recommended decision the Board adopted, reasoned that because appellant took
charge of carrying the weight bench into the gymnasium with the assistance of the students, he
should have anticipated the dangers involved in this work, including the risk that the bench would fall
on his foot, and therefore, his accident was not “undesigned and unexpected.” However, it could as
well be said that a librarian who re-shelves books should reasonably anticipate that if this activity is
not conducted properly, the book shelf could fall, that a social worker who transports a child to court
should anticipate that if she is not careful getting into or out of her car, she could catch her hand in
the car door, and that a gym teacher who does not look at the ground while walking should anticipate
that he or she could trip on a riser or other object. Yet the Court recognized that such work-
connected accidents could constitute “traumatic events.” Thus, it is clear that an accident can be
“undesigned and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in
retrospect that the employee could have anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to
avoid it.

[Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284.]
See also Minosse v. Bd. of Trs., PFRS, TYP 8553-11, Initial Decision (January 4, 2012), adopted, Bd. of Trs. (February 14,
2012), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/> (traumatic event was undesigned and unexpected where police officer was
injured when he kicked open a barricaded door and struggled with a suspect after being dispatched to a domestic-violence
location). Therefore, the potential foreseeable consequence of the occurrence does not make it undesigned and unexpected.
Accordingly, under the facts and circumstances presented here, I CONCLUDE that petitioner’s disability directly resulted
from a traumatic event that was undesigned and unexpected and, as all of the other requisite criteria have been met, his
application for an accidental disability pension should be approved.
DECISION AND ORDER
Therefore, the decision of the PFRS Board to deny petitioner’s application for accidental disability retirement benefits is
hereby REVERSED. I ORDER that petitioner’s application for accidental disability benefits be APPROVED.
I hereby FILE my Initial Decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN’S RETIREMENT
SYSTEM for consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND
FIREMEN’S RETIREMENT SYSTE, Mwhich by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of
Trustees of the Police and Firemen’s Retirement System does not adopt, modify or reject this decision within forty-five days and
unless such time limit is otherwise extended, this recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with
N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
Within thirteen days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written
exceptions with the DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF PENSIONS, One State Street Square, 50 West State Street, P.O. Box 295,
Trenton, New Jersey 08625-0295, marked “Attention: Exceptions.” A copy of any exceptions must be sent to the judge and to
the other parties.
